pe_section: My part is pushing the envelope: finding workloads that serverless platforms handle badly, and explaining exactly why they fail on each platform.
pe_sofar: We ran on AWS Lambda and on a self-hosted OpenWhisk, and used plain Docker as ground truth, because there we set the CPU limits ourselves and can check every mechanism in isolation. I added three benchmarks to SeBS: an OpenMP stencil that also measures how much CPU it really gets, ResNet-50 inference with ONNX Runtime, and data-parallel SGD. Plus two experiments that run them as sweeps. Every run records its commit and raw data. Two findings: thread oversubscription and gang scheduling.
pe_cpus: Lambda gives you CPU in proportion to memory: one full vCPU at 1769 MB. But at every size we tested, the function sees two CPUs. At 128 MB it really gets 8 percent of one. The limit is enforced by the hypervisor outside the VM, so nothing inside, not even a cgroup file, shows it. On about 40 percent of invocations the hosts give even less, the green line. Thread runtimes like OpenMP and ONNX Runtime size their pools from the CPU count they see, so they oversubscribe by default. ONNX Runtime is worse: pinned to two of 32 CPUs in Docker, it still starts 32 threads.
pe_storm: Oversubscription alone would be cheap. The problem is that these runtimes busy-wait: an idle thread spins instead of sleeping. On a dedicated core that is fast. Under a fractional share it burns exactly the budget the other thread needs to reach the barrier. Here I keep the total work constant and only add barriers. At 128 MB the same computation becomes 58 times slower with two threads, and long runs hit the 300 second timeout. At 1769 MB, a full CPU, there is no penalty. Passive waiting halves the time.
pe_onnx: Same effect in a real application: ResNet-50 inference. ONNX Runtime's workers spin by default, and more threads make it up to six times slower, at every memory size. Its default of two threads already costs 16 to 34 percent below 1769 MB. On OpenWhisk with a 4-CPU quota it starts 32 threads and is 11 to 18 times slower. Turning spinning off brings every thread count back within 25 percent of the best. Nobody does that by default.
pe_gang: Second finding: bulk-synchronous jobs. Distributed SGD needs all ranks running at the same time, and FMI from this lab assumes exactly that. We measured when it stops holding. A run completes exactly when N is at most the platform's concurrency cap. On AWS that is the account limit, 10 for us. On OpenWhisk it is invoker memory divided by action memory, so doubling memory halves the cap. The cap predicted all 60 launches. The failure looks different per platform, on the right: AWS rejects the extra ranks, and the running ranks wait until the timeout, billed. OpenWhisk queues them silently; they start only after the others gave up, and no error is raised. Even below the cap, ranks spend most of their time waiting at barriers.
pe_next: Next: our account is capped at 3008 MB. Above that, Lambda reports more vCPUs while the share stays continuous, so oversubscription could come back at large sizes. We want more runtimes, OpenWhisk on Kubernetes where CPUs are pinned, and gang scheduling with asynchronous invocation and larger N. Finally, GPUs on a self-hosted OpenWhisk, whose scheduler only looks at memory.
